utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody. Madam Registrar, could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am. All the accused are here. Amongst the Defence teams, I notice the absence of Mr. Bourgon, and that's it. Prosecution it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. And Mr. Tansey, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANSEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you just acknowledge your presence in the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TANSEY
utterances.text: Yes, my name is Rock Tansey, and I'm counsel on behalf of the witness Momir Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You're welcome. Any preliminaries? None. I think we can proceed, then, with bringing in the witness. Oh, I see, I was wondering why everyone was looking at that door instead of the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome once more to this Tribunal where today you've been summoned to give evidence by the Trial Chamber itself. You're familiar with the procedure. Before you start your testimony, you are required under our rules to enter the solemn declaration that you are familiar with. Please read it out aloud and that will be your undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me explain to you very briefly what's going to happen today, and I would suppose the next few days. We have a few questions for you, following which we will then hand you over to the Prosecution and the various Defence teams that might be interested in cross-examining you. At the end of that, you can go back to where you came from. Judge Prost has been delegated by us to put a few questions to you. Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, good morning. With reference to --

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: -- your original statement of facts which you filed with the original Trial Chamber in your matter, it was filed on the 6th of May, 2003, I am asking you whether you confirm that original statement of facts with the qualifications that you have provided in the statement of facts -- the further statement of facts which you filed with this Trial Chamber on the 17th of April. Do you confirm both of those statements of facts?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Judge Prost, before you proceed, there was one further thing I wanted to draw your attention to which I forgot, and that is you would have noticed in the courtroom the presence of Mr. Tansey, your lawyer. He will be looking after your interests here during the course of your testimony. You cannot communicate with him, of course, but he is free to make representations if there is anything that you feel ought to be brought to our attention. Thank you. Yes -- sorry, Judge Prost. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And in respect of those two statements, those constitute your declaration, and can you confirm that were you to be examined on those statement of facts directly today that you would give the same responses to any questions as you provided in those two declarations?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. And on the basis of that confirmation, the Trial Chamber is admitting into evidence the original statement of facts attached to the plea agreement in relation to the case of Momir Nikolic and the further statement of facts of the 17th of April, 2009, filed before this Trial Chamber. Mr. Nikolic, you will be aware of the fact that the Trial Chamber on the 2nd of April, 2009, issued you a - what is referred to as a subpoena duces tecum - in which we asked you to bring with you to this court today relevant documents including the personal notes that you made in the preparation of your defence. Can you advise whether you have brought any notes with you here today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And can you indicate if you are prepared to produce those notes for the parties in the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Certainly, I don't object to that. It's a folder containing around 100 pages, and I have no problem with anyone having insight into it, making photocopies of it. There is nothing special in it, and it contains the information that I received from the OTP; and I have really no objection to anyone looking into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Madam Usher -- Mr. Nikolic, Madam Usher is going to take the documents from you for a moment. The Chamber is going to have a look at the materials that you have produced. To the Chamber, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just say two sentences as means of explanation of what this is all about. This document or these preparations that I made while I was preparing myself for the trial, this folder contains analyses, and 90 percent of them are actually statements of potential witnesses proposed by the OTP. The rest of the material constitute orders, statements, and other documents that I also received from the OTP; therefore, there is not a single document in this folder that I had received from other sources other than the OTP, and I analysed them. This is my personal analysis. How competent it was, how relevant it was, it is not up to me to say, but I have nothing against anyone making copies of it and presenting it to anyone who is interested. And I don't think that the Defence will see anything beyond which is contained in the folder that they already have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. We will have a look at the notes and we may have some additional questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Having heard the witness's affirmation, is anyone one of you Prosecution and Defence teams, interested in these notes? Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yes, good morning. Yes to look at them, if we may, at least, just to take a look at them. But also, Mr. President, there are other notes in front of the witness and just to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are aware of that, we were precisely discussing that. But we were undecided as to whether we should deal with that ourselves or whether you should deal with it. Once you have raised it, I think we can deal with it straight away. Judge Prost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, as counsel has just noted. You appear to have some additional materials with you today. Can you advise us at as to what other materials you have with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that this is your ruling ordering me to appear before the Court, and what am I supposed to do and expected to do once I am here. This is another ruling instructing me to bring the material that I have as a kind of working material that I had prepared before the trial. Here I have a statement of facts and acceptance of guilt, so that is effectively the first statement that I signed. The next document is an addendum to the statement that I sent to you and that you have in front of you, and it contains corrections and amendments in compared to the old statement. The next document is an extract from the book "Command and Control," published in 1993. The next document is my letter asking for legal representation and assistance in the process of the preparation for my trial. The next document I received from the OTP, and it pertains to the composition of the teams who took part in the negotiations in Bratunac while meetings in Bratunac were taking place. The next one is my letter to Mr. Tansey asking assistance in my writing a statement. There is another statement of -- as well. There is also a document that refers to my medical condition in 1992 when I was in hospital. These are the statements given by the Muslims who were willing while -- during my preparations to come forward and testify in my trial, and some of the statements of Muslims who provided statements about me and my character. So these are all available for inspection. What I have here is a document relating to cooperation. In a word, all of these documents are also in possession of the OTP. So this is cooperation between the Bratunac Brigade of the Republika Srpska and the battalion while they were in Potocari and Srebrenica. These are some requests that I have for my lawyer. This document is also in the hands of the OTP, and that's the record of the hand-over of items from the vault of the security organs. And this is my letter written to my lawyer which I need here. This document speaks about the engagement and daily deployment of Milici police. So these I believe to be crucial documents, but I have nothing against the Defence team looking at them. I am not using -- not going to use anything other than the statement of facts and the plea agreement. The only document that I need is this statement that I will probably or possibly use during my testimony, as for the rest of it, I won't need it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. As far as we are concerned, that's the Trial Chamber, we are not interested in any of these documents. Of course, we do understand any requests that Prosecution or Defence might make in relation to some or all of these documents should you think you are required to see them. Thank you, Mr. Nikolic, for bringing all of this material with you. We are circulating the notes that he referred to earlier and which we had a quick look at. The intention is to have them photocopied. And, as it is, my suspicion is that although they might be of interest to some of you, they might not be of interest to others; so if any of you is absolutely not interested in having a copy, please let us know. It will spare us having to photocopy all those pages unnecessarily. Okay. Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Out of an abundance of caution, we have been discussing the desirability of keeping for the time being, at least, the notes, treating them as confidential in order to avoid the possibility of leakages in relation to witnesses, et cetera. So your responsibility is to keep them, for the time being, treat that document as a confidential document, and then we'll decide later on what the position ought to be. Okay. Judge Prost, again my apologies to you for all these interruptions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, we just have a few questions for you following up from the statements which have been filed before us. And initially, I'm going to address this question to Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Ostojic, Ms. Nikolic. In the content of the statement of facts produced by the witness, there is reference therein to Vujadin Popovic, Drago Nikolic, and Colonel Beara. Now, without, of course, addressing the substance of what is alleged to have been said or to have been done, I want to know from counsel whether there is any dispute that the references to those three individuals are references to your respective clients; and I also wish to know whether you take any issue with Mr. Nikolic's ability to identify those three individuals. Perhaps we will start with you, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you ask me about the reference of my client and ability of Mr. Nikolic to identify him?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Yes, I am asking you, Mr. Zivanovic, whether you accept that the references that Mr. Nikolic makes in his statement of facts to Vujadin Popovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: -- are, in fact, references to your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: You accept that fact?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And you don't dispute Mr. Nikolic's ability to identify your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Ostojic, the references to Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: You dispute the references to Colonel Beara as being references to your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Ms. Nikolic, do you dispute the references to Drago Nikolic as being references to your client?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And you accept that Mr. Nikolic is in a position to identify your client?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can identify my client. Of course, I dispute the context in which my client's name is referred to in the statement of facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you. Then dealing, Mr. Nikolic, in your original statement of facts - and I can refer you particularly to section 10 of the statement of facts - if you want to have reference to it. You indicate that: "In the evening of the 13th of July, I was having dinner at the Bratunac Brigade headquarters when I received a call from a communication room to report directly to Colonel Beara in the centre of Bratunac. I travelled to the centre and met with Colonel Beara at about 2030 hours." Mr. Nikolic, at the time did you know Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: You had met him on previous occasions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And what position did Colonel Beara occupy at the time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Colonel Beara, at the time, was the chief of security administration at the Main Staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And the Colonel Beara that you are referring to, is he present in court today?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, he is present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And can you just, for our purposes, identify where he is seated?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Certainly. He's in the back row, the second person -- or, rather, the person next to Mr. Popovic. There is Mr. Popovic and Mr. Colonel Beara.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Nikolic, in your statement of facts you describe a conversation that you had outside the Hotel Fontana on the morning of the 12th of July. This is a conversation, and this is in section 4 of the second paragraph, a meeting you had with Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic and Lieutenant-Colonel Kosoric, during which conversation you are told about the intention to separate the able-bodied Muslim men and to execute them. So you have that knowledge as of the morning of the 12th of July. Now, you then spend, according to your statement of facts, much of the day on the 12th at Potocari assisting in that separation process and working with others in dealing with the movement of people and the separations. You describe in particular working with Dusko Jevic, did you discuss with him that day the fact that the men, the able-bodied men being separated were to be killed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, no. Not in the sense that we discussed it directly. In my statement, and in my previous testimony, I said that I was in contact with Dusko Jevic being the only officer I had contact with. At a certain point in time I assisted with what the problem was at the moment, and it had to do with the buses and the transport of people. It was Dusko Jevic who was tasked with that. Therefore, I did not discuss any murders with Dusko Jevic. Everything else, this separation and the other things that were taking place, were obvious. Everyone could see that, including myself. In my statement, I referred to the way I was in contact with Mr. Dusko Jevic, and I also said that he was the only officer I had contact with. I also stated that I assisted him in transporting the people from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: At the same time on the same day you speak about working with others in what was going on in Potocari, military and MUP units, Drina Corps military police, you've listed a number of individuals in section 6 of your original statement. On the 12th, did you have any discussions with any of those individuals about the fact that these men were to be killed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no. Not on that day in front of the Fontana or at Potocari. I did not have any contact with or talk to any other participants in the operation of the transportation of people from Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: So you're saying that neither on the 12th nor on the 13th during the course of that activity at Potocari, on neither day did you have any discussion with anyone about the fact that these men were going to be separated and killed?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No. I never testified to that effect, and I never mentioned it in my statement. I never said that I discussed the murder of those people with anyone in Potocari. As I explained, the next day on the 13th, since on the 13th I was in Potocari briefly, I stated that I saw Dusko Jevic again. By mere circumstances, the military police of the Bratunac Brigade was working there together with the unit commanded by Dusko Jevic, or the unit that he worked with. On that day we met only briefly and then I left Potocari, and on the 13th, I did not return.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prost. Mr. Thayer, cross-examination, if you have any. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, and good morning to and Your Honours, good morning everyone. Mr. President, I do have cross-examination for Mr. Nikolic. I think I will be taking the allotted time to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nikolic. Allow me to introduce myself. My name is Nelson Thayer, I will be asking you questions on behalf of the Prosecution today.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to begin by showing you a log-book I believe you'll recognise, that you are familiar with. I have the original here, I don't know if you have your glasses with you. You may need them. I think the original will be easier to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: It is 65 ter -- actually P00220.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I would just ask you to take a look at it and see if you can recognise what it is.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: What is the number of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: This is our exhibit number for this trial, P0220?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understood. I do recognise the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: These are the daily reports of the MP detachment -- platoon, of the 1st Light Infantry Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What I would like to do with you, sir, is just go to a couple of entries in this log-book and ask you some questions about them. If you could turn to the page for the 12th to 13th of July, and you may recall you can probably see that the dates are in the upper left-hand corner. This is on page 16 of the original B/C/S in e-court, and that's page 13 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The 12th and the 13th of July, 1995. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, there is a reference here to the UNHCR - there are a couple of references, in fact - indicating that the military police were securing the UNHCR at the school. And I think you've told us before - and I'm just asking you to clarify before this Trial Chamber - whether that reference to UNHCR is correct or if that refers to some other entity that was being secured at the school by the Bratunac Brigade MPs?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I think -- or, rather, I'm absolutely positive that this is a mistake of the policemen who made the entries. They did not distinguish members of the UNHCR and members of the DutchBat, who were in Bratunac at the time. This is, as a matter of fact, providing security to soldiers, members of the DutchBat, who at the time were billeted at the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And which school was that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: They were billeted in the Djuro Pucar Stari high school in Bratunac, that is the only high school or mid-level school there is in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we could turn to the page for the 14th to the 15th of July, and this is at page 17, just the next page in B/C/S in the e-court, and 14 in the English, sir. Do you see the entry for the 14th, 15th of July?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is a reference here to - and I'll just quote: "The police was engaged in the escort of Muslim refugees." What's that a reference to for this date, the 14th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the 14th, in the morning, the police of the Bratunac Brigade or its parts took part in the transfer of Muslim refugees as part of the convoy which was departing for Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you refer to "Muslim refugees and convoy," who are we talking about, sir, more specifically in terms of these Muslims; and where were they before they were brought on this convoy to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This has to do with the Muslims who on the 12th and 13th of July were separated in Potocari. It also includes the Muslims who, on the two days, were captured along the road Bratunac-Kravica-Konjevic Polje and subsequently transferred to Bratunac. All those Muslims, the captured ones, who put in the Vuk Karadzic school building, as well as the other facilities, all of them were transported on the 14th onboard buses and trucks to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could just turn the page, please, to the next entry, and then one more page to the entry for the 17th of July, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is a reference here in the log to: "One police patrol remained in Pilica to secure and guard the Muslims." Can you tell the Trial Chamber what that refers to and how you know that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I made a slight correction in the additional statement of facts. It is a matter of terms which, however, do not change the essence of what took place. A patrol of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade on the 17th of July remained in Pilica in order to secure the captured and detained Muslims in the facilities in Pilica. I learned of that subsequently, not on the same day, not on the day when they were held there, but later, from the commander of the MP platoon of the Bratunac Brigade, Mirko Jankovic, who told me that a patrol remained there. What was the other part of the question? I think there was something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Actually, there wasn't, sir, you've covered it, but I do have a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How much later from this day did Mirko Jankovic tell you that a patrol had remained in Pilica?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you precisely. Perhaps a day or two later. I truly cannot recall. I do not remember the exact date. In any case, immediately afterwards, one or two days at the most after they were held there.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to look at just one more entry in this log. If you could - and this is at page 24 of the original, and it's -- should be the last page in the English, page 21. I think it's an additional translation that was done. And, sir, I'd ask you to look for the entry for the 23rd and 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There is a reference here to six Muslims who are brought in and are now in custody; two other Muslims were brought later but sent back to Skelani because they had cut their throats, so they were sent back. What can you tell the Trial Chamber about these two prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Nikolic. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is not an objection. It seems that the date on the English version and the B/C/S version do not correspond. In B/C/S, it says the 22nd and the 23rd; whereas in the English we have the 23rd and 24th of July, 1995. I do believe that the body of text is the same, but that there is a mistake in terms of dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So according to you the correct dates are 22nd and 23rd, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I thank my friend. That is a simple mistranslation in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's not a mistranslation it's the wrong page, they showed the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it was the wrong page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. Thank you, Judge Kwon. Mr. Thayer, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I reply? Regarding the two captured Muslims who were brought to the Bratunac Brigade, it concerned the following: They were captured, as far as I know, in Skelani, by the Skelani Battalion. The commander of the Skelani military police brought them to the Bratunac Brigade wanting to hand them over. I did not allow that. The MP commander spoke with me, and I told him that the two detainees were not to be put in custody or detained there, but that they should see a doctor, that they should go to the health clinic. They were in need of medical assistance, not to be put in I gaol. I don't know what the fate of the two men was. I do know that they were not handed over to the Bratunac Brigade. They put them back in the vehicle they had come with and took them away. That's what I can tell you about the two Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, sir, we are done with that document. You can close up the log and we'll move on. Thank you. I want to turn your attention to the period of time immediately before the Serb forces entered Potocari. Did you have an occasion to be at Zuti Most at some point at Yellow Bridge prior to the Serb forces actually entering Potocari and, if so, did you meet with any VRS or MUP commanders at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Could you be more precise, if possible? I met people at Zuti Most a great many times. If you have the dates of operation in mind, then I can tell you that on the 11th of July at Zuti Most, I met with Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about that meeting? How did it come about and what happened?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On that day, the 11th, I was notified and told to come to Zuti Most. I was told that Colonel Borovcanin was there with part of his forces that accompanied him. I arrived there some ten or 15 minutes later, Mr. Borovcanin asked me or, rather, we talked about where were the positions, the targets of Muslim units that could be seen from Zuti Most. This was supposed to include the targets on the left-hand side of the road and the right-hand side of the road in the direction of Bratunac and Srebrenica. To be specific, on the left-hand side it was the village of Likari and the positions and fortified positions there. On the right-hand side of the road, it had to do with the village of Budak where also there were fortified Muslim forces. There were bunkers, fortified buildings, et cetera. The basic reason why Mr. Borovcanin asked me to tell me about that was that I was the chief of the security intelligence organ at the Bratunac Brigade, and I had information where certain fortifications were. As for why Mr. Borovcanin asked me that was to engage the targets directly from the area of Zuti Most. That is basically the long and short of it. I did indicate to him the positions I knew about, and the information that I had concerning the enclave. Mr. Ljubisa Borovcanin then subsequently engaged the targets using a T-55 tank. I also need to add that at that time when Mr. Borovcanin was firing at those positions, I subsequently learned and had information that on the 11th in the afternoon, at those positions there were no longer any Muslim forces left.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just a quick follow-up, sir. You referred to Mr. Borovcanin as Colonel Borovcanin. Is that how you knew him at the time, by that rank?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, I think he was a colonel with the police, but, however, I am not absolutely sure. I do believe that this was -- he was addressed in that manner by his soldiers and by the people who knew him, but I am not sure which ranks existed in the police at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Turning your attention to that evening, sir, I want to see if we can get a sense of what the intelligence picture was that you had going into the evening of July 11th. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what information you had regarding Muslim men in the area of Potocari and what, if anything, you did with that information that night?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: On the evening of the 11th or, rather, in the afternoon as well, a large number of Muslims were walking towards the UNPROFOR compound, and they eventually arrived there in Potocari. Some previous information that we had and the current information also received from reconnaissance units from the battalions and units who were in direct contact with the Potocari sector indicated that among the civilian refugees from Srebrenica there was a large number of Muslim men in Potocari, among them those who were fit for military service. According to our estimate, and I underline these were our estimates as well the estimate of those people who were working on these issues and directly observing this whole process, say that there were between 1.200 and 1.500 able-bodied Muslim men. I can explain to you very briefly on what our estimates were based. For a very long time there were 50, 60, even 70.000 men at one point in the area of Srebrenica, and I am talking about the municipality of Srebrenica. Of course, such a large number of able-bodied men, due to the lack of weapons, were not militarily engaged in units, but they were fit for military service. So on the basis of this estimate we assessed that at the time between 1.000 and 2.000 able-bodied men were in Potocari. All this information received on that day, primarily from the 2nd Infantry Battalion, and that was the battalion in direct contact with the Potocari compound and that area, therefore, this information plus an analysis of the overall situation prevailing on the evening of the 11th, I put together into an intelligence report which through usual channels I faxed to the intelligence service's department -- intelligence and security department of -- of the Drina Corps. I also orally informed one member of my command, and that also happened on the evening of the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And just briefly, sir, who was that member of your command?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That evening, I informed members of the command who were present in the Bratunac Brigade HQ, these are staff officers who were part of the corps command. And, of course, all this information and intelligence was relayed to my commander as well, which is absolutely a regular procedure, and I'm talking about my commander, Vidoje Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, during this period of time - and I'm talking about the Krivaja 95 operation and the days immediately following - there was a Main Staff intelligence officer by the name of Colonel Radoslav Jankovic present in your brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And where did he make his office during this period of time?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: During that period, Colonel Jankovic was sharing an office with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And during the 11th of July, did you share this information regarding the number of Muslim men in Potocari directly with Colonel Jankovic, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, there was no need for me to convey this information to Colonel Jankovic because Colonel Jankovic was aware of all the information that arrived in my office and vice versa. So he knew absolutely everything that was happening in that period on that day or that evening, and he knew everything about the manner, time, and content of my report going out into the superior command. And you can see it from the documents, we very often worked together on these reports. So, Mr. Colonel Jankovic wrote his reports from my office and sent it out in the name of the organ for security and intelligence affairs of the brigade. In other words, Colonel Jankovic knew about this information and about the overall situation in the -- in Potocari at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, going into the morning hours of 12 July, sir, [French on English Channel].

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll keep trying, still French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If that could be corrected, please. It's not that I don't like French, but. All right. Is it okay, now? I don't think we are receiving interpretation in French anymore now. Let's proceed, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Again, focussing on the intelligence picture that you had going into the morning of 12 July, had you received more information about the whereabouts of the Muslim men from Srebrenica that morning?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, already in the morning of the 12th and later on, even more intensely, information started pouring in that elements of the Muslim forces who were pulling out towards Muslim-controlled or free territories were in the Jaglici and Susnjari sectors, and that they are using this axis for pulling out of Srebrenica. Yes, we did have this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And presumably that information is being received and then sent up both the intelligence chain as well as the command chain so that the appropriate individuals and organs are notified; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I want to spend a little bit of time with you, sir, discussing this conversation that you had with Colonels Popovic and Kosoric in front of the Fontana before the third meeting in the morning of 12 July. You've already spoken a little bit in answer to Her Honour's questions, but I want you to please, if you can, provide as much detail as you can for the Chamber about how this discussion came about.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to explain in detail in order to avoid any you misunderstandings. What happened in front of the Fontana was in no way a meeting. That's the first thing that I would make -- or like to make clear. So at 10.00 on that day, that was on the 12th, a third meeting had been set between the Dutch battalion, representatives of the Muslim side, representatives of the civilian authorities of Bratunac, and representatives of the MUP, police, and Army of the Republika Srpska. You know who participated in this meeting. I can give you these names, but I don't think it's necessary. Immediately before the meeting started, Mr. Popovic was supposed to take part in this third meeting and we met each either in front of the Fontana Hotel for a very short period of time, five minutes, seven minutes, but not more than ten minutes. That's how long we spent in front of the hotel. And the conversation went more or less like this: I asked him what was going to happen next. I knew all the details about the situation, and I heard at the previous two meetings what the plans were and what the general mood was. Mr. Popovic answered that probably the Muslim forces or, rather, the civilians, women and children, and people who are not fit for military service, that this whole population would be transported to the Muslim-controlled territory which implied the town of Kladanj. He also said that the so-called screening would be carried out in order to separate able-bodied men, to identify those who had committed or who are suspected of committing war crimes, et cetera. However, at this point in time, I really have to provide an additional information. After all this, something happened that was absolutely never planned nor did I grasp from my conversation with Mr. Popovic that something could happen. Except in the first convoy, our -- not only able-bodied men were separated, but all, all men who were in Potocari were separated from their families and put on bus -- actually, first detained in Potocari. Therefore, I asked Mr. Popovic what was going to happen to these men because, to be honest, not even then I couldn't -- could understand why these men were being set aside. What was the purpose of all that? I was given a simple answer, Popovic told me in his usual way of putting things: All the balija have to be killed. That was, in a nutshell, my conversation with Popovic. In light of the circumstances and the situation that these men were going to be separated, I said that the only area in Bratunac where it is possible to detain these Muslims after they had been separated were the facilities in Bratunac, i.e., Vuk Karadzic elementary school, the hangar, and some facilities situated in that part of the town. All those who were separated in Potocari were, indeed, transported and detained in the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, in the old school in Bratunac, in the hangar, and other facilities located in this district of the town. This is what happened. A similar conversation took place after the meeting between myself and Mr. Kosoric. He also kept saying that all the Muslims will be deported to Kladanj, that the screening will take place in order to separate the able-bodied men and those who were suspected of being war criminals, and as I said, this conversation is almost identical to the one that I had previously. One more thing happened at that time is the following, but of course it took place after the meeting, and that is that I had a conversation with two officers from the Dutch Battalion. They asked me, Mr. Nikolic, what is going to happen next? I told them everything is settled, everything is regulated, the buses will be here and you go back to Potocari and wait for the buses. This would be briefly the summary of my conversation with Mr. Popovic. Before the meeting, Mr. Petar Sumljic [phoen] was also present there, including later two members of the Dutch battalion with whom I spoke after the meeting at around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to go back and focus on your statement of facts. If you have it there, and this is at section 4 of the statement of facts. And that would be -- and this is 65 ter 4489 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can anyone -- yes, but can anyone identify the source of this noise, if it's near enough to him? Just want to make sure that it's not some kind of gas leak or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's safe advice. We'll have a break now for 25 minutes. Thank you. But also we need to establish whether the noise or whatever is also in there where the accused and the witness are being kept, because if it's something that needs to be attended to I want to make sure that they are safe. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Thayer. You've been putting questions for 44 minutes already. May I just remind you that this is not a direct. You are cross-examining the witness, and you are entitled to go straight to the point if you so wish, instead of going around in circles. Yes, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, let's go straight to where we were before, which is section 4 of your statement of facts regarding this conversation that you had with Colonel Popovic before the third Fontana meeting. Have you had a chance to read that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in the statement of facts, you're very clear that: "Popovic told me that the thousands of Muslim men and women in -- Muslim women and children in Potocari would be transported out of Potocari towards Muslim held territory near Kladanj and that the able-bodied men, Muslim men, within the crowd of Muslim civilians would be separated from the crowd, detained temporarily in Bratunac, and killed shortly thereafter." That's the way the conversation happened, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. What you have just quoted, I said a minute ago as part of the explanation that I provided in response to your question. Maybe not in so many words, but basically this is what I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, there was one thing I was a little bit confused about your answer before we broke. You made a reference to Muslims who were being permitted to leave on the first convoy on the 12th of July. I just want to make it clear, this conversation that you had with Colonel Popovic before the third Fontana meeting happened before any of the convoys left Potocari; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And it is also correct, is it not, that as you told the RS [sic] Commission in answers to their question, this is at paragraph 26, you first realised that the Muslim men would be killed when you spoke to Popovic during this conversation; that's correct too, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. That's when it dawned on the me for the first time, and I think I was right in understanding the situation like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, in the -- in your Trbic testimony - and this is at pages 29 and 30 for my friends - you made some references to Mr. Popovic and Mr. Kosoric being agitated and angry when they were talking about the Muslims having to be killed; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I do, but I don't remember in which particular context I said that. I can only repeat that not only Mr. Kosoric and Mr. Popovic were agitated, angry, and nervous, everybody else was nervous, I, myself, included; and the answer is that all these people who you have mentioned were both nervous and angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: But I just want to make sure that we are clear about this conversation, sir. Your understanding during this conversation was that Colonel Popovic and Colonel Kosoric were looking for detention facilities as well as execution sites; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't use -- I have -- I received translation that they were looking for detention facilities. A short while ago in my testimony, I said that it was me who suggested and told them that there are facilities which were ear-marked for detention of the Muslims, i.e., the Vuk Karadzic elementary school and the other facilities that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how about the Ciglane brickworks factory and the Sase mine location that were suggested as execution sites. Was that something you just came up spontaneously with, or were you asked to provide potential sites for the execution of the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nothing in similar, nothing specific, no requests or suggestions were made. Quite simply, we discussed the issue and I, along with the two of them I mentioned as the locations where these men separated in Potocari and were temporarily detained can be executed. I manage -- I mentioned the brick factory and the Sase mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Subsequent to this conversation, you had a conversation with Colonel Jankovic after the third Fontana meeting.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, your statement of facts indicates what the task was given to you by Colonel Jankovic, and you've expressed in your amended statement of facts that very clearly that you were not acting as a commander and were not in a position to coordinate anything in the sense that coordination implies elements of the command function. Do I have that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, for the record, Prosecution agrees with you, sir, that you were not a commander during this period of time. What I want to do is turn to your statement of facts - and this is 65 ter 4483, the amended statement of facts. And I'll just read two sections to you. And this is at page 3 of the English: "As a reserve captain I neither coordinated nor supervised the transportation. That could only be done by high-ranking officers from the Drina Corps, the VRS Main Staff, and the RS MUP who had the power to issue orders and make decisions on their own." And then further down you state that: "The commanders or forces engaged in Potocari did not do anything to prevent their own units over which they had control and which they supervised from committing these abuses." When you speak of the commander, sir, who exactly are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the commanders of units that were engaged in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you give us any examples that you know by name?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can give you the name of the units that were engaged in Potocari or elements thereof. Of course, I know the names of the commanders, or a number of them; I don't know exactly who the commanders of the other units were. I can mention and enumerate the units that I can positively say were present in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think you've done that in your statement of facts, so we don't need to repeat that there.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just want to turn your attention back to Colonel Jankovic of the intelligence organ, and I'll just go directly to the document. It's 65 ter 260.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it. I know which document we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we - and I would want to clarify two issues with respect to this document, sir - if we go to the last page of the handwritten document in the original, at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we can scroll down to the bottom of the original, all the way down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There are some initials there. Can you tell us what those initials are, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I see the initials Radoslav, maybe Jankovic, I think that's Colonel Jankovic's initials in the left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So that would be RJ, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this last paragraph, Colonel Jankovic is asking what to do with the MSF and UNPROFOR staff. And this is again the last page in the handwritten and paragraph 3 of the English. When you were interviewed in 2003, you told us that what Colonel Jankovic was asking about here was to either let these individuals be evacuated or have them joined -- join the other separated Muslims. Do you remember telling us that, sir? That that's what this memo is about, and if you want I can take you to the transcript page for it, but do you remember telling us that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I do. I remember well what I said. I still assert that what I said then was true, and I can confirm that here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what is also true that you told us back then was that Colonel Jankovic understood, and this is the reason why he was asking so specifically, was that the men among those individuals who would be separated, if they were to be separated and not evacuated, would be killed. Do you remember telling us that as well, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I still think the same thing. If you were to ask me that now, I would offer the same opinion. Had they been separated they would have been killed, much as the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to ask you some questions now, sir, about Potocari. You told us already that you were dealing with Dusko Jevic, and as far as you understood his immediate superior was Colonel Borovcanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber with respect to the men who were being commanded by Colonel Borovcanin and Dusko Jevic who were at Potocari, what was the chain of command that was operating at that time? In other words, who commanded those special police brigade forces and other MUP forces who are in Potocari during the separations and transportations on the 12th and 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Sir, it's a difficult question to be put to me. I'd rather not go into commenting on the line of command and control in the MUP. The only reason why I don't want to talk about it is because in principal I know how it worked, but precisely and accurately as regards the mutual relationships within the chain during the operation, that is something that I am not fully familiar with. I am only familiar with it generally speaking, and probably it applies to Potocari as well; but it is for that reason I would kindly ask you not to require from me to define the system of command and control of the MUP, because I am not fully familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Don't worry, sir, I am not asking you to be a MUP expert. We've already heard from a couple of those guys. What I am asking you is, for example, were you in command of these special police brigade forces in Potocari on the 12th and the 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was not in command of any brigades or units, police units, that were engaged in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: To your knowledge was anyone from the Bratunac Brigade commanding the MUP units in Potocari on the 12th and 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: What was your understanding in terms of the respective chains of command, not in terms of the intricacies of how they were operating, but in terms of how the various units were operating together in Potocari? How were the members of these individual units, for example, the special police brigade, the Drina Corps MPs that you saw there, the Drina Wolves that you saw there, how were they receiving their orders in order to know what to do in Potocari on the 12th and 13th?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'll try to the extent possible for me to explain what you are asking. According to the things I know, in Potocari there were certain units of the special forces, the special forces brigade, of the MUP. What I know is that the commander of the forces from the special MUP brigade was Mr. Borovcanin. In addition to the special MUP brigade units in Potocari, there was also the police of the so-called -- well, they were called PJPs. PJP units had their own commanders. They had their own "komandir" and "komandant" who was in command of all those PJP forces. As regards any other units in Potocari at the time, the battalion of the Bratunac Brigade had its own commander who was in direct command and control of the battalion pursuant to the brigade commander's orders. Then there were units from the Main Staff that were directly subordinated to their own respective commanders from the areas they had arrived from. There were parts of the 65th Protection Regiment that were subordinated to the commander of the regiment, i.e., the commander who was present in Potocari. As for all other units from the Zvornik and other brigades, they had their commanders. They were directly answerable to the commander of the unit engaged pursuant to brigade commander's orders. In principal, that is what I can tell you about it. What I think is this: Control over all MUP units, I may be wrong in saying this, but this is what I think, control over the units of the special MUP brigade as well as the PJP units and the police units from the public security station in Bratunac, as well as all other police forces engaged in Potocari and in its environs, in my belief were under direct command -- sorry, control of the chief of the centre, Mr. Dragomir Vasic. What General Krstic had within his purview as the command of the corps in terms of military forces, the same applied to Mr. Vasic when it came to police forces. That was my understanding of the engagement and command in the operation of evacuation from Potocari. That is my view about the way these units were engaged and commanded over within the police structure and military structure. All forces that were engaged in the Srebrenica operation, and the operation of forcible transfer from Potocari, were commanded and controlled by the Chief of Staff General Krstic and the commander of the Drina Corps. Of course, once General Mladic was in the field in the area of Bratunac, then, of course, it was well known that it was General Mladic who made decisions, ordered through his subordinate officers, those being commanders of the corps, brigades, and all other units that took part in Operation Srebrenica. That is, in short, how I understand the chain of command and control of the units engaged in Operation Srebrenica and during the transport operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And so just to tie that up, based on what you observed and what you understood, you had Colonel Borovcanin commanding, controlling, Dusko Jevic. How does he fit into Dragomir Vasic and his command and/or control?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Mr. Nikolic. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all that question misstates the answer. And, secondly, that's now the third time that my learned friend has referenced my client as Colonel. The witness's answer on that point was clear, and I object to that being repeatedly put in the record what that does not reflect what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we don't need any comments on your last remark, but in relation to the alleged misstatement, what do you have to say, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I am simply following up on this answer that the witness gave about his understanding of how it worked based on his experience there. He's talked about Mr. Vasic, and I think the natural follow-up question is, Okay, well, how did the men that you saw on the ground in Potocari fit into that? I think it's a perfectly natural follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Its not a question of whether it's a natural follow-up question, it's whether you are making a statement which reflects truthfully and faithfully what the witness has stated or whether you are twisting it somewhat as Mr. Gosnell is suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he -- again, go straight to the question you need to ask in relation to the possible relationship between Borovcanin and Dusko Jevic according to the transcript. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll repeat my last question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How did Mr. Borovcanin and Mr. Jevic fit into this command structure as you understood it with Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to answer that how Mr. Borovcanin fit within the command structure. It is my view that it was standard structure prescribed by -- under law that was in place. I see no other logical explanation. In my view, the chief of centre, if I compare it to the army, what is within the remit of the security centre would correspond to the territory, perhaps not all of it but more or less the same territory under control of the corps commander. All forces within the area of the corps commander are subordinated to that corps commander. He is the boss and he is answerable for the actions of his subordinates. I apply the same logic to the MUP. If there is a chief centre [as interpreted] in Bratunac and there were commanders of the brigade special forces of the MUP that were introduced in the area, as well as PJP units, which were at the level of the centre in terms of staffing, then the security stations and all of their forces, if we take all that into account, it is my conclusion that that relationship was the one that would be logical and valid within the framework of the MUP forces present. I cannot arrive at any other conclusion, and that is all I can tell you about it. I may be mistaken. I have to reiterate I am no expert. I am not knowledgeable on MUP structure. I don't know what the relationships are within the chain of command, control, resubordination, et cetera, et cetera. I am not familiar with it to the extent needed to meet the requirements contained in your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's move to Konjevic Polje --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, before you do so, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption. Apparently, there is either a transcription or translation error at page 37, line 1. Instead of "If there is a chief centre in Bratunac," apparently the words were "If the chief of the centre is in Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's move to Konjevic Polje. You refer in your statement of facts to seeing Nenad Deronjic there on the 13th of July. How did you know Mr. Deronjic to recognise him, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I knew Deronjic firstly because I used to be his teacher; secondly, because he is a local. He hailed from a village that I hail from. I had known him from civilian life, and I used to be his high school teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And at the time were you aware that he was a member of the 2nd Company of the Zvornik PJP, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I did not know that he was a member of the Zvornik PJP company. I did know that he was a member of the police force without knowing which unit he belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you also referred to another individual named Mirko Peric, and who is he and how did you recognise him?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was another police member. I think he belonged to the public security station in Bratunac. I have known him for a long period of time. He is senior to me, and I had known him as a member of the police station in Bratunac. I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And from what you could see, sir, both of them were there in their official capacities as police officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so. They were engaged there, and I saw them there when I was going to Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You also refer to taking Resid Sinanovic to Bratunac and leaving him with Zlatan Celanovic, a lawyer who is attached to the Bratunac Brigade military police platoon. Can you tell us a little bit about what you understood Mr. Celanovic's position and duties to be?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can. The light infantry brigade, that is to say my brigade was a light infantry brigade. In terms of establishment it had two functions: The intelligence and security one. And there were organs, respectively. Under law, I as the person representing the intelligence organ in a light infantry brigade was not an authorised official. I had no authority to conduct any affairs dealing with criminal law, and that should be clear straight away. Mr. Celanovic was engaged pursuant to an order and decision of the brigade commander. He was in charge of all procedure that had to do with collection, processing, and preparation of all criminal reports for certain crimes committed by members of the Bratunac Brigade or that they were suspected of committing. In addition to that, in terms of percentages, in some 90 percent of the cases, he also conducted interrogations of the prisoners of war and all those who were brought in under that status. Based on that, he would compile minutes and reports that he would send to the commander. What was of interest to me as the security organ -- well, he would forward to me such type information. There are countless examples of that. I received a number of criminal reports by Mr. Celanovic and reports on similar matters within the framework of the brigade. To put it briefly, that was his main task.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Thayer kindly speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, while you were at Konjevic Polje you had an encounter with General Mladic. Can you tell the Trial Chamber about that, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. I encountered General Mladic in Konjevic Polje on the 13th of July. After 12.30 or so, the time may have been half an hour prior or later, but it was within that period that General Mladic came. I went out, I greeted him, briefed him, and the obligation number one for me - and it is why I had gone to Konjevic Polje the first time around - to check the safety of the road to be travelled by General Mladic. I told him that things were fine, that there were no problems, and General Mladic spent some time in Konjevic Polje. He talked to a group of captured Muslims who were in Konjevic Polje then. After that, he told them that they shouldn't worry, that things would be fine, and that they were to be transported safely to their desired locations. After that conversation with them, he moved about that area and he went back to his vehicle. I asked him then, General, sir, what are we going to do with these people? Because from one moment to the next there were more and more people who were captured. There were men, of course, there were those who had surrendered, and when I asked him, General, sir, what is going to happen with these people, General Mladic made a gesture. He did this. There was no other comment on his part. He just made a gesture and that's it. And there was no other conclusion I could draw other than those people being -- that they were going to be killed, and that is precisely what took place in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And for the record the gesture you are describing is one of drawing your hand from left to right, palm facing down, just straight across chest level; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I saw. That is what he indicated then. Two minutes later he was in his car and went on from Konjevic Polje onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, when you testified in -- in the Blagojevic trial, and this is at page 2245 of the transcript for my friends, you stated that: "I understood that to mean that those men would be killed." And then you went on to say: "Actually, I saw that to be a confirmation of what was already happening." Can you explain that to the Trial Chamber a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: There is nothing in terms of details that I can add. He indicated it, and in my view it could mean nothing else as was confirmed later. He meant precisely that. I have no further explanations to offer. It is perfectly clear to anyone familiar with the gestures used. I see no need to offer any other explanation. It is certainly clear to me as well as to all the others who saw me making the gesture. It is clear what the General meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just to clarify for the transcript, it says: "The others who saw me making the gesture," it was General Mladic making the gesture, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I did not play that role. I had no authority. I was not in a position. Everything I said had to do with General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We believe the witness was indicating himself as far as the gesture made in the courtroom now meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, my question more specifically, sir, was when you testified that you saw this gesture as a confirmation of what was already happening, what were you referring to when you said that you saw it to be a confirmation of what was already happening?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it was a confirmation of what was going on in Potocari on the 12th. In other words, all the men who had been separated were already detained, so it was crystal clear only people who didn't want to understand that couldn't understand what the fate of those separated men would be and what the intention behind the separation was. According to what Mr. Mladic and in the way in which he reacted made it clear that there would be no difference in the fate between those captured in Konjevic Polje and those who were already detained on the 12th and separated and that the same fate awaits them as that of those who had been separated and detained in Potocari. This is what I had in mind and that's what I said then and that's what I'm saying now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Just so we are completely clear, what is that fate, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, their fate was that they would be put in detention and later executed. That was the fate awaiting the men who had been captured on that road.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you testified in the Blagojevic trial about the trips that you were taking back and forth along that road on the 13th from Konjevic Polje, from Bratunac to Konjevic Polje, Konjevic Polje back to Bratunac, and again. You testified that on route to Konjevic Polje you saw forces deployed at Sandici and all the way to Konjevic Polje and that those forces were under the command of Ljubisa Borovcanin. And that's at transcript page 1712. Can you confirm that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, the forces engaged between Sandici and Konjevic Polje were, in my understanding, under the command of Mr. Ljubisa Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the immediate commander was Dusko Jevic - correct? - as you've testified in Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You will have to be more precise, I don't know exactly what I said on that occasion. Immediate commanders were unit commanders of the units that were engaged in that area. I may have said that Dusko Jevic was a superior officer to the units from the special MUP brigades, the units that had come from Jahorina, and that is true. Dusko Jevic was a superior officer to the companies of special police that had arrived from Jahorina. There were two companies, however, their commanders were Mendeljev and Mr. Nedjo Ikonic, if I remember correctly. So these two commanders were directly in command of the companies while Dusko Jevic was somebody who had control over these two companies, and the commander of these forces was Mr. Borovcanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sir, just to clarify one thing. The last name of the company commander whose first name is Nedjo, do you recall -- can you repeat what the last name of the commander Nedjo was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nedjo Ikonic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the last name of the commander whose first name was Mendeljev, what was his last name?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I only know him by the name of Mendeljev.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay. I want to take you to the evening of 13 July. You've already spoken a little bit about Colonel Beara. Can you tell the Trial Chamber - and I won't review the account in your statement of facts, just to save a little bit of time - but when Colonel Beara told you that the prisoners were going to be transferred to Zvornik, had you heard that before or were you learning it for the first time in your conversation with Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was the first time that I heard that the prisoners from Bratunac who had been separated in Potocari and temporarily detained in Bratunac would be transferred to the territory of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And when you drove up to the Zvornik Brigade command that evening and then subsequently to the forward command post, can you tell Trial Chamber, please, in as much detail as you can remember, what your conversation was with Drago Nikolic at that IKM.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That was a very short meeting. Drago Nikolic and I did not discuss any specific topics. I conveyed to Mr. Drago Nikolic only the order issued to me be Mr. Ljubomir Beara. I said to him that I had been sent by Mr. Beara to convey his order, that members who had been separated, i.e., the men from Bratunac who had been separated and housed in the facilities in Bratunac, would, during the day, be transferred to Zvornik and that his task was to prepare the facilities and men who will receive these prisoners. This is what I conveyed and that was actually more or less the content of the order that I had received from Colonel Beara. I also told him at the end, because this conversation between Drago Nikolic and me didn't last longer than five minutes, I turned my vehicle, Drago came out in front of the forward command post, I told him what I had to tell him, conveyed the order, and I also said that I had information that these men who were being brought or taken to Zvornik would be executed. This is what I said to Drago Nikolic. After that, I sat in my car and returned with my escort to the command of the Zvornik Brigade. This is where I dropped off the policemen and that same evening, I proceeded back to Bratunac to the command of my brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And the information that those prisoners would be executed, that was part of the order that you received from Colonel Beara to transmit to Drago Nikolic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Well, it was both information and order and everything that was at that point in time already clear to everyone. On the afternoon of the 13th and on the evening of the 13th, it was clear to everyone - of course I am referring to those who wanted to see things - that these men who were separated were going to be put to death, and it was clear to everyone, including myself. I passed on information that I had information that these separated men were going to be executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did Drago Nikolic say to you in response to this order that you were conveying from Colonel Beara?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drago Nikolic made no comment at all. He simply said, since he was at the forward command post, he said that he was going to report and inform him command and then see what happens next. Of course, it was only to be expected and it was only logical that he was going to carry out the order that had been issued, but specifically Drago Nikolic didn't say anything about that apart from the fact that he was going to report to his command and act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, after you returned to Bratunac that evening, you reported -- you reported back to Colonel Beara that you had fulfilled the task that he had given you and passed the order to Drago Nikolic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And then Colonel Beara summons you to a meeting at the SDS offices of Mr. Deronjic as a -- as you've stated in your statement of facts; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber where physically you were during this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The premises where the meeting took place is made up of two rooms. One room is an office with a desk and the rest of it. The second room, or the other room, had a small desk in it and where the secretary of the president of the SDS was sitting. These two rooms have adjoining doors. At that meeting that evening, my task was and I was requested to go to the SDS office where we found the president of the SDS, Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, there was also Mr. Beara, and Mr. Vasic, the chief of MUP, was there as well. I did not take part either in the meeting -- the debate or the discussion directly. I was sitting there in the office of the secretary and the -- this communicating door between these two rooms was simply open all the time. At the beginning, there were arguments and there was shouting between Mr. Deronjic and Mr. Beara. After that they all sat down and continued to talk normally: Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, Mr. Beara, and Mr. Dragomir Vasic. Everything that I said about what they discussed and talked about is contained in my statement; therefore, I am reluctant to repeat that, and I can confirm it today if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, why do you think it -- according to you Mr. Beara summoned you to this meeting if you are not taking part in it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I was born in Bratunac. I took Mr. Beara to the offices of the SDS because, I suppose, that he didn't know, or perhaps he did, but the only reason was that the fact that Mr. Beara didn't know where the SDS offices were. I can only construe it that way. As for my participation in the meeting where you have the chief of the security administration, the chief of the security centre, and the deputy or Mr. Karadzic, is not such a level of a meeting that I would be expected to make contribution to. The man superior to me was Mr. Beara, so there was no place for me to take part in a meeting where my boss from the top echelon of the army is present. Therefore, I didn't take part in this meeting in any capacity, but I did have an opportunity to hear everything that was being discussed. Now, if you're asking me whether it was necessary to discuss these problems because there were huge problems in Bratunac, the risks were high, the situation was terrible, and nobody slept that night; therefore, it was necessary to undertake measures to try and place in a way everything under control because everything was out of control and there was total mayhem and anarchy in every respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I may ask you the question myself or Mr. Thayer could take over from me.
