In page 46, lines 6, 17, and 18, you are recorded as stating here in the transcript: "At the beginning, there were arguments and there was shouting between Mr. Deronjic and Mr. Beara. After that they all sat down," et cetera, "and continued to talk normally." What were these arguments and what was this shouting about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point was the status and the fate of the prisoners who were in Bratunac and who, on that night of the 13th, were still arriving in buses and trucks from the direction of Konjevic Polje. Miroslav Deronjic, as far as I could hear, asked for all these prisoners to be taken away from Bratunac and that no executions take place or abuses take place in Bratunac. He didn't want them there any longer. That was his viewpoint. During the conversation and this argument, he invoked the decisions issued by President Karadzic saying that he had received instruction, from President Karadzic how to deal with the prisoners who were at present in Bratunac. Colonel Beara invoked the instructions he received from his boss. I am not going to guess who his boss was, but I can only imagine; and he claimed that he had totally different instructions how to deal with prisoners who were in Bratunac at the moment and who were arriving from Konjevic Polje by the minute. So these were the issues that they started arguing and quarrelling from the very outset. Later on, they sat at the table and started discussing all other issues, such as how to secure the men who were there, what to do because Bratunac was full of buses, trucks with captured Muslims brought from Konjevic Polje, Bratunac. All the facilities were fully packed, including the Vuk Karadzic elementary school, the hanger, and all the other facilities. And they were full of captured Muslims. This created a security risk for the town. So there was total chaos. Nobody knew how to secure these people, and the situation in the town of Bratunac became intolerable. Later on, they tried to find a way to provide additional forces and men who would secure the buses and the trucks, the schools, the hangar, the secondary education centre; so they were looking for ways of preventing any incidents because incidents were already starting to happen. People were taken off the buses, and there were individual killings. As I said, the situation was very bad. It was horrible both in the town and in the facilities where the detainees were being kept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic. There are two further short questions I would like to put to you in relation to what you have just testified. Line -- page 48, lines 9 to 12, you said: "During the conversation and this argument, Deronjic invoked the decisions issued by President Karadzic saying that he had received instructions from President Karadzic how to deal with the prisoners who were present in Bratunac." Can you be more specific? Did he explain, did he specify what these instructions from President Karadzic were in relation to prisoners with being brought or being present in Bratunac at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Miroslav Deronjic, in addition to other things, but the most important request that he made, and let me be quite clear, invoked not the decisions but the instructions that he had received. I don't know the nature of these instructions, I've never seen them. I suppose that those were instructions passed on to him orally because I had never seen any such instruction. So he invoked the instructions received from President Karadzic, and the essence of these instructions was that the prisoners from Bratunac be transferred to Zvornik. That was the essence of it. Mr. Deronjic insisted that no single man should be executed or killed in the territory of Bratunac municipality. Whether he knew more than that, I'm -- wouldn't like to speculate, but this is -- and I'm just conveying to you what I heard with my own ears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And on a similar matter, then you continued saying: "Colonel Beara invoked the instructions he received from his boss. I'm not going to guess who his boss was, but I can only imagine, and he claimed that he had totally different instructions on how to deal with prisoners who were in Bratunac at the moment and who were arriving from Konjevic Polje by the minute." So was he specific? Could you enlighten us on what -- on the essence or the nature of these instructions that Beara claimed to have had received from his superiors, from his boss?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I honestly cannot because Mr. Beara never mentioned the content of the instructions received from his boss, but it was evident that they were different from the instructions received of him from Mr. Deronjic; and that is what created a clash between the two; but I cannot say that he the ever went into any details about the instructions that he had received from his boss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, let's not dwell on the details. The fact is from what you were overhearing, Colonel Beara was arguing with Mr. Deronjic, and Colonel Beara was talking about his orders to have these orders killed; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In my statement -- in my first testimony, actually, I said about this meeting what you just mentioned. That was a meeting where it was openly discussed what the fate of these prisoners would be or, in other words, about the killing of these prisoners. Miroslav Deronjic - what I managed to overhear - opposed this idea of these men being killed in Bratunac. The fate of these men was at stake, and they wanted to make a decision what to do with them. Miroslav Deronjic was opposed to the idea to keep these men in Bratunac any longer and to be executed in Bratunac. That was the essence of the discussion in this meeting. And for the first time, I was present at a meeting where the killing of these men in Bratunac was openly discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And Mr. Deronjic indicated, did he not, that he was going to report back to President Karadzic regarding the outcome of this meeting and the discussions?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I don't know. Whether he sent in reports or to whom he sent any reports, whether Mr. Deronjic sent a report to his president, whether Mr. Beara and Mr. Vasic reported to their superiors, I don't know. I never saw such reports dealing with these matters; and, therefore, I cannot confirm. All I can say is what I already told you, and that is that during the conversation they invoked in the instructions given by their respective superiors. That is what I saw and heard. Whether they wrote subsequent reports or not and sent them to their superiors, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, sir, I am not specifically referring to written reports. I am simply referring to the discussion from what you overheard entailed these participants indicating that they would inform their superiors of the outcome of this discussion. Whether or not it was in written form, it was clear to you that the participants had their respective superiors to whom they were going to report on the outcome of these discussions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can only assume that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, sticking with the night of the 13th of July and what was going on in Bratunac, specifically the facility of the Vuk Karadzic school, the old school, and the hangar there, you received some information from Dragan Mirkovic concerning the number of Muslims who were killed that evening, who had been detained in the hangar and in buses in that area; did you not?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I subsequently learned what took place on the 13th of July in the evening in the hangar and the buildings there. I never mentioned -- well, as far as I know, the murders did not take place at the Vuk Karadzic primary school. The murders took place at the hangar and its environs. According to what I know, there were no murders in the school, murders of those who had been captured and accommodated there. The information stated in the statement of fact is correct; and that is to say, that I learned from Dragan Mirkovic later that in that part of the hangar that between 80 and 100 people were killed in his assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And how soon after these events did Mr. Mirkovic give you this information?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: A while. It wasn't 7 or 15 days later, but after an interval. I can't say precisely how long, but it was a bit after the event of the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I want to skip ahead a couple of days, sir. You are familiar with a sweep operation which took place on -- beginning on the 17th of July in which Captain Mico Gavric had been designated coordinator of some mixed forces including those controlled by Dusko Jevic; do you recall that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in the course of that operation, some boys were separated out of the adult prisoners and taken to the Bratunac Brigade. You recall that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: How many boys do you recall arriving at the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Three or four, I really don't know. I think there were four boys. I'm not sure. I was never much interested in that issue. I only heard that some children were brought there. I didn't see them or talk to them. I suppose there were three or four.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's take a quick look at 65 ter 257, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: There should be a document appearing on your screen in a moment, sir. We also have a typewritten version if that's easier.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I can see it and read it. There were four minors between the ages of 8 and 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you recall learning that these four children were filmed for propaganda purposes during this time as indicated in this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Nothing more than what you've said. In a conversation with Mico Gavric, I learned that during a joint search the forces of the Bratunac Brigade, working together with the forces commanded by Dusko Jevic, captured some 35 to 38 members, Muslim men. I also heard from Gavric that -- Mr. Gavric, as well as the commander of the unit taking part in the search, that they handed over those captured to Mr. Jevic. After the search, the 35 to 38 men were handed over to Mr. Jevic. I don't know what their fate was after that; therefore, I cannot offer any comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gavric testified that you were the duty operations officer that day and that you told him that a bus would arrive from the Bratunac Brigade to transport those prisoners. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, I think that was an error. I wasn't duty officer on the 17th of July. I was duty officer between the 12th and the 13th of July. I'm not certain -- or, rather, I simply don't know of this alleged fact that on the 17th I was duty officer. I cannot exclude that possibility, however. If I talked to Mr. Gavric on the bus -- or about the buses, maybe I did mention something to the effect that buses would be arriving. I really don't know. In any case, it wasn't up to me to secure transport. I really cannot recall and cannot comment. I don't think it is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I see we are at the break. Or are we going to continue until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have another ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but we can have the break at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's fine. I'll keep rolling, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is it okay with everyone? Okay. Let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Do you recall what capacity during this time-period of the sweep your brigade had to transport prisoners, sir, in terms of available vehicles, buses, trucks?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In a brigade, one could find a bus available any time for people to be transported. It is my conclusion to move 35 to 38 people you only need a bus, and one could always come up with a bus. That's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, let's look at 65 ter 258 very quickly, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have an urgent communication here from your brigade command to the corps indicating that it doesn't have a single motor vehicle suitable for the transport of wounded Muslim prisoners, here 23 Muslim prisoners. Does that help you recall whether or not during this period of the sweep your brigade had adequate vehicles to transport prisoners captured during that sweep operation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't received interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked if we can ask the witness to take off his headphones before I continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, he's understood. [French on English Channel] ... the headphones on his ears in any case because what Madam Fauveau is going to state will be translated into English. I think he does. Do you speak English, Mr. Nikolic? Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how do you communicate with other people where you are being detained at present, not in this country, elsewhere? In which language do you communicate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not. No language is used. I simply do not communicate with others. When I need medical assistance, then use is made of an interpreter via the phone from a distant town to assist me with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Thank you. Please remove your earphones or headphones. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The question has been put in such a way that it could lead to some mistakes. We are talking about carrying wounded people and that there is no vehicle that is adapted to transported -- to transporting the wounded and not the prisoners. As it was mentioned in the previous question, I was talking about 35 to 38 prisoners. Of course for the wounded, you need specific vehicles for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Madam. Do you wish to comment, Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think that was an answer that he can certainly give himself. He's capable of answering the question based on the document, and I think we are just about to get there. He can say whatever he wants about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can safely go ahead and then if we have problems, we'll review this matter as we go along. Thank you. He can put his headphones on again. Mr. Thayer, if you could repeat the question, please, or simplify it maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, just really quickly, when you look at that document does that help at all refresh your recollection at all without the capacity that your brigade had for transporting prisoners during this sweep operation?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, it does not help me. In the document you are showing me, deals with a request for a vehicle that would be suitable to transport the wounded Muslims; therefore, the request has to do with an ambulance. It is true that the Bratunac Brigade did not have such a vehicle at its disposal with which it would have been able to transport 23 wounded Muslims that had to be transported. That's what I can tell you about this document. I still assert that on the 17th of July the Bratunac Brigade could provide a vehicle, but this request has to do with a special-purpose vehicle, an ambulance which wouldn't be needed to transport those wounded Muslims. That's all I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So the bottom line is ultimately you don't know who's vehicle was used to transport those prisoners to wherever their destination was; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: From this document, one arrives at a clear conclusion. The request was sent to the Drina Corps command asking that they urgently provide a suitable vehicle to transport 23 wounded Muslims. It was sent to the corps command, and the corps command from their own resources were supposed to deal with the issue of transport of the 23 wounded Muslims. That's all I can read from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's put the document to the side, sir. I am talking about those 35 or 38 prisoners that the special police brigade had in their custody in Konjevic Polje. I just want to find out, and then we'll move on. Do you have any idea who's vehicle it was that transported those prisoners to wherever their destination was. If you do, you do; if you don't, you don't.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I really don't. I know nothing beyond what I heard from Mico Gavric.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Did Mico Gavric ever tell you what his understanding was of what happened to those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: No, we never discussed their fate. I don't want to speculate in order to guess at what happened. I can come up with a number of conclusions, but I cannot know what happened with them reliably. If they are no longer among the living, then we know, but I don't want to speculate. I don't want to draw any conclusions of that sort because I am truly not familiar with their fate.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you told us in your recorded interview with the OTP in 2003 that, and this is at pages 118 and 120 of that interview for my friends, you told us that during these sweep operations in the aftermath of the fall of the enclave, that small groups of prisoners were being killed summarily during the sweep operations. Do you recall telling us that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: In the course of those sweeps, as I said, groups were being killed. What I had in mind then, as I do now, were those groups that put up resistance and were subsequently killed in combat. If I said anything otherwise, then I apologise. Then there was a misunderstanding. It is those groups that I had in mind. Throughout the searches, there were activities, clashes, fire being opened at each other. If I said anything to the contrary or if I misunderstood, I apologise. In any case, this is the type of killing I had in mind. In a conversation, I also said the following: That those who had been captured and are now no longer among the living, and if they are not among those captured and then put on the lists of various prisons and were subsequently released, if the people we are talking about had been captured and then went missing, then we can reliably conclude that they were killed. And this is what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We can have the break now. It will be of 25 minutes duration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understand that the Borovcanin Defence team would like to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'll be very brief. The Prosecutor has just been pursuing a line of questioning whose purpose seems to be an attempt to implicate Dusko Jevic in relation to a sweep operation on the 17th of July. Now, if that is the purpose of the line of questioning that has just been pursued, and if in term that purpose is some how related to a suggestion of the criminal responsibility of my client, then we object on grounds of the relevance to the indictment and object on the grounds of lack of notice. There is absolutely nothing about in the indictment, no material fact is alleged in this regard. So we object on that ground; however, if there are some other purpose, if it's relevant in some other way, or perhaps if they have no more questions on this area, then there is no need for a particular response. But then again, Mr. President, we are ten weeks away from a final brief being given. It might be nice to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have an absolute right to know, actually. Yes, Mr. Thayer is the only person who can answer that, apart from Mr. McCloskey, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have moved on from this specific sweep on the 17th, and Dusko Jevic's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You do concede what Mr. Gosnell has claimed, namely, that there is no allegation of Mr. Borovcanin's involvement in the particular event that you are asking the witness about?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: In the indictment, we do not have Mr. Borovcanin specified. I think, especially through the evidence of the Defence witness Mico Gavric we spent some time on this sweep issue, and frankly that is the direction in which I was taking it. I was less concerned about the MUP folks as I was about other issues, and I've moved on. I'm still talking about what's happening in the sweeps in general, that's where I'm going, but it's -- it's not focused on Dusko Jevic or Ljubisa Borovcanin. It has to do with a general activities that were underway --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- consonant with our theory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. That puts your mind at rest, Mr. Gosnell, at least for the time being. Yes, let's bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May I proceed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I just want to pick up where we left off. You had told us about in the circumstance where prisoners were captured, and they -- their names show up on a missing list. In those cases, you could deduce that there had been a summary execution. I want to take you back to what you specifically told us in this recorded interview, and I'll just read to you the question and answer during the course of the interview, and you can tell us whether this is what you have in mind. You were shown a Bratunac Brigade daily combat report, and there is a reference to, and I'll quote: "A small part of the enemy force are still surrounded in the area of Bokcin Potok." And Mr. Nikolic asked you the question: "So over the next few days were the prisoners still being captured in this area?" Your answer was: "Yes." And for my friends, this is at page 119 and 120 of the 2003 interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY ASKED
utterances.text: "And what was happening to these captured prisoners?" And your answer was: "They were killed and no one of them were brought. As far as I know, no one was brought and detained." Mr. McCloskey followed up and asked: "Where were they killed?" And you answered: "Probably in the place, the various places where they were captured." Now, my first question is: Do you recall that question and answer, and do you stand by your statements there?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall it, and I stand by my statement. I would like to clarify, briefly if I may. The way the questions were interpreted to me appeared quite hypothetical in their nature to me. As I said then and I do now, I believe that during the searches when people were being captured in the course of combat, I have no information that the people who had been captured in the area of Bokcin Potok and elsewhere of them being brought to the Bratunac Brigade. The question is: What happened with them? Logically, if they were not brought to the brigade and they are no longer alive, of course they were executed in situ. That is certain. I was not a witness to that, I did not participate in the sweeps, but I state with certainly that those people who were arrested there, captured there, without being brought anywhere were killed. That is my final answer. I have nothing else to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And particularly in your role of intelligence chief for the brigade, and just given the amount of information that you were receiving during this period of time, you were picking up information, were you not, whether it was a specific site or otherwise, but you were hearing reports of such summary executions following the fall of Srebrenica during these sweeps. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We only disagree in the part referring to any reports. Never in any report did I see which stated that anyone was liquidated. However, we do agree that the people who were captured there and who did not appear anywhere else, i.e., that there is specific information that people had been captured and later on went missing, I agree that they were killed onsite.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And let me just show you one document on this issue, and then we will move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: May we see 65 ter 4486, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And I'll just give you a moment to reacquaint yourself with this.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We have here a 19 July report from Dragomir Vasic, and it's regarding activities of MUP forces, and this is in the area of Crni Vrh and Snagovo. Again, during -- on the 19th, and it refers to: "Eight Muslims soldiers were neutralised. We learned from them that some 200 Muslims armed with automatic and hunting rifles are located in the sector below the old road near Snagovo." Referring to learning information from -- eight Muslims soldiers were neutralised, suggests, does it not, that these prisoners were executed in situ?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I will strive to be precise. The area of the sweep was not in the AOR of the Bratunac Brigade. That was the Zvornik Brigade's AOR. I understand the contents of the report, however I think it would be wise for me not to draw any conclusions about the documents since I don't know anything about it. I would decline to comment because I was not familiar with the situation, I don't know what took place, although I could draw conclusions. A general conclusion would be in all matters similar to this is that people who have been captured and went missing later on are dead, killed. That's all I can tell you. Don't ask me to arrive at any other conclusions, because I did not have information about this. I think it is the first time I see this document, and I do not wish to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Let's move to the reburial operation, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And if we could have P00219 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And sir, I have the original, I think it will be easier for you to look at. So I ask Madam Usher to kindly hand that up to you. Thank you. Do you recognise what this document is, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what it is, please.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: This is a document which contains reports or briefings from the meetings of the 1st Bratunac Light Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn your attention to the entry for October 16, 1995. If you could find that. That's page 24 of the B/C/S on e-court, page 11 of the English translation. And I would draw your attention, sir, when you find the October 16th page to the -- towards the bottom of the page. If you look at the bottom of the page, sir, there is an eight-digit number. Have you found it? October 16th.

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've found it. 16th of October, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Under your name, it says: "We are currently engaged in tasks issued by the Army of Republika Srpska Main Staff." And then you've written a word in place of in parenthesis. What is that word, sir?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Let me just first correct you. It wasn't me who wrote this. This was written by the minute taker, but these are my words quoted here. Yes, it's correct, we are currently engaged in tasks issued by the Main Staff of the Army of VRS, in parenthesis, "asanacija," in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And what are -- what you are referring to here, sir, when you wrote "asanacija"?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the task that was underway in those days, and it involves the removal or relocation and re-digging of graves from the area of Glogova village and relocations to secondary graves in the area of Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And why did you report at this command meeting that these reburial tasks had been issued by the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Because at the very beginning of this operation, I heard from both my commander and Mr. Popovic that this task had to be carried out and that it had been ordered by the Main Staff of the VRS. So this is the information that I heard from Mr. Popovic and Mr. Vidoje Blagojevic. I just need to add one thing more, for clarity. The operation of relocation of graves was dubbed, in my brigade, under the title of "asanacija." I don't know who designated this terminology, but I was instructed to do so. During conversations and debriefings with my commander, I always used this term.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And based on your experience in the military, what was your understanding of the regular usage of the term "asanacija" to mean?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, "asanacija," and in my view this is not a proper term. I know exactly what "asanacija" of terrain involves and what it means, but in this particular instance, it is not entirely proper. But, on the other hand, it envisaged certain sweeping of the area, of the terrain, and removal of things -- of something that existed there. Under normal circumstances, the "asanacija" of the terrain would involve the moping-up of the battle-field where operations had been carried out before, including the removal of the dead, the burial of the dead, or the people or the dead animals. So the "asanacija" of the entire battle-field would be an effort to bring this area into its previous state. That would be the shortest explanation of what true "asanacija" involves. In this case, this involved relocation, the bodies buried in this big grave to secondary graves in the area of Srebrenica municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, how this task was given to you by Colonel Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I'm going to be very accurate. Mr. Popovic and I had a contact sometime in September, I don't know exactly the date or the day, in my brigade; but I know that it was sometime in September. Mr. Popovic said on that occasion that there was an order from the Main Staff for the relocation of the grave in Glogova. Furthermore, he told me that pursuant to this order, the command of the Drina Corps received an order to initiate the whole action and that the task of the Drina Corps command or the security organ of the Drina Corps precisely to ensure, for this operation, the necessary quantities of fuel and that this fuel provided from the resources of the Drina Corps should be stored into proper storage areas or gas stations, and that the security organ of the brigade, that is me, had the task to monitor the consumption of the fuel. After the task had been completed, my duty was to send a written report justifying the use of petrol and fuel oil that had been received from the Drina Corps. And, of course, in view of everything I have just told you, I can tell you that I had never seen a written order to this effect. I never discussed this with my commander asking him whether he had such an order or not, but judging by the reaction of the my commander, I am convinced and I am sure that the same order went down the command line and that my commander knew what the next task would be with relation to the re-digging of these graves. I can also add that after this, my commander and I simply did everything that we had been asked to do in relation to these reburials, and this operation involved a lot of people, a lot of resources, assets, vehicles, and everything else that was needed. And to put it simply, this task took a long time to complete, perhaps even the whole month with some interruptions. About everything that happened, I reported to the commander of the Bratunac Brigade at meetings, which is evident from this record. And, finally, all the tasks given to me, primarily to take care of the fuel, I supported by provided books to the Bratunac Brigade showing all the quantities of fuel used, and we were obliged to replenish these quantities that were used. After the operation was over, I packed up all these books and sent it to the brigade. One copy was left in the safe of the security organ. There were also some other documents, such as working log, records of the vehicles, records of people who were involved and participating in the operation. In a word, everything that had to do with the operation and its execution. This is what I can tell you to the best of my recollection about all this.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You told us, sir, that you were convinced that your commander had received the same order that you did concerning the reburial operation. Why are you convinced of that?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I was convinced because, at least in my Bratunac Brigade, nothing could have happened without the knowledge of the commander. It was impossible for a security organ to do something or to use the brigade resources or to use the MP unit that I used, for example, to use vehicles or any other resources without the approval of the brigade commander. That was practically impossible scenario. Furthermore, I am also convinced due to the fact that my commander knew, and I can say for certain, more than I knew about the organisation, the preparations, the resources, the assistance that we expected to come from the engineers battalion of the Drina Corps regarding the engagement of machines, et cetera. All of this indicated to me that my commander was aware of this task, that he knew what was to be done, and that he knew who he was to cooperate with in performing this task. Therefore, I am absolutely convinced that he knew about this before I knew anything about this. And I feel the need to say one more thing. This operation was allegedly to be a covert operation, so secret operation. However, everything that took place during the operation in view of the number of men who were involved, the number of vehicles, the number of machineries; the number of laborers who were engaged to work, the people who were engaged to provide security, meaning from the civilian structures, police, military police, of army; everything that took place there cannot be and could not be kept a secret despite of the original intention. As it turns out, everything was done openly, overtly, and publically, and in a nutshell everyone knew what was going on and what was being done.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I want to switch topics now and go back a little to the months preceding the Krivaja 95 operation. I just want to reorient your recollection a little in that direction. You testified in the Blagojevic case, and this is at the transcript page 1635, that the final objective was to make life unbearable for the people in the enclave, to make it impossible for them to live on, and as a consequence people would then eventually leave the enclave. And I want to spend a little bit of time talking about what your brigade did, for example, in connection with achieving that objective prior to the Krivaja 95 operation. For example, you testified in Blagojevic about sniping into the enclave prior to the Krivaja 95 operation. Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the sniping from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. In this testimony of mine, I spoke about a number of circumstances that led to a conclusion to be made that the ultimate goal was to create intolerable conditions, and thus obliterate the population of the whole enclave. The sniping had to do with members of the Bratunac Brigade and units that were in direct contact. Actually, they were the ones who were encircling the enclave. Of course, it was -- this was not only the Bratunac Brigade, there were other units there deployed on the border with Srebrenica, and primarily this was the Skelani battalion and -- and the Milici Brigade. During the period when Srebrenica was declared a demilitarised zone, this problem became more prominent. During that time, I was a communications officer in the Bratunac Brigade; and most of the time I contacted with the DutchBat officers as well as representatives of all other international organisations operating in Srebrenica. I was constantly being criticised, and I think justly criticised, for the sniping activities targeting the targets that were not of military nature. These problems involved shooting from snipers on people beyond the lines, and in most cases those were civilians working in the fields or doing some other business. I, myself, did my best the prevent this, but I wasn't very successful because quite simply there was no cooperation in many segments regarding this issue; and we do not all agree that the sniping should not take place and that civilians should not be targeted. So that was one of the segments which was conducive to the creation of a difficult life for people living in the enclave, by preventing them from doing their everyday works and duties. There was the attitude towards civilians, but there were also aspects or other activities that prevented representatives of the Dutch battalion and the international organisations who took care of the situation in the enclave. There were such acts that contributed to the fact that these international organisations and Dutch battalion become or were rendered incapacitated for carrying out their mandate in the enclave. First of all, I have in mind the absolute and total blockade of -- put on supply lines, first of all to the Dutch battalion, starting from food, weapons, equipment, ammunition, and everything else that in total contributes to full combat readiness of a unit and its capacity to do its job that it's deployed to do. This blockade was effected by stopping the entry into Srebrenica by convoys, the prevention of rotation of units and companies that were replaced periodically, preventing the supply of fuel for PCP -- APCs, and other vehicles that the Dutch troops had. There were also other attempts to prevent them from going at meetings -- to attend meetings with their command in Sarajevo, et cetera, et cetera. I believed at the time that that was a very unfair and unprofessional attitude towards them. And, of course, I must clarify one more thing, and that is the conduct of my commander. Before the attack on the enclave was launched, I am talking about Mr. Ognjenovic, in an information in which he addressed members of the Bratunac Brigade, everything that I spoke about as kind of a negative occurrences and unacceptable behaviour, he described in his information; and he asked them to make the people for -- make the life for people living there even worse and to create such intolerable conditions that would force them to leave the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, before we break let's look at P03177, please. And I have the original here for you if that helps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer, he was talking about Mr. Blagojevic instead of Ognjenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can he confirm --

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Well, I'll let the witness develop this point, and I think we're going to answer your question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've seen it. So, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, you referred to your commander as Commander Ognjenovic. When he was commander of your brigade, sir, if you can just roughly give us the years?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I don't know the exact period, but definitely sometime in 1994. He was my commander on two occasions, but I'm quite sure that it was in 1994 and for some period in 1995; but I don't know is the exact dates of his coming and going because he was appointed twice, and he was removed twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's fine, Mr. Thayer. I can see his name at the bottom of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 2 of this document, sir, your commander wrote: "There will be no retreat. When it comes to the Srebrenica enclave, we must advance. The enemy's life must be made unbearable and their temporary stay in the enclave impossible to that they leave the enclave en mass if possible realising that they cannot survive there." And just prior to that he wrote: "We must continue to train, arm, discipline, and prepare the Republika Srpska Army for the execution of this crucial task for the expulsion of Muslims from the Srebrenica enclave." Is this an example of the type of report that you are referring to, sir, that displayed the attitude of your commander?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is what he wrote in this information. He signed it. And he insisted that what he wrote be put into practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And you testified in Blagojevic that this specific report had an effect on the sniping that was going on. Just quickly, can you describe what that effect was?

utterances.speaker: MOMIR NIKOLIC
utterances.text: As I said, it was the obligation of our battalion and unit commanders to acquaint all soldiers with this information sheet. The commanders organised briefings, they briefed the soldiers in terms of the contents of the document. And the soldiers, of course, saw this as a support to the things they have been doing, irrespective of group of officers in the Bratunac Brigade who were strongly against the sniping and making the life of people in the brigade -- in the enclave unbearable. Many or most of the soldiers simply saw their previous behaviour being encouraged, and they behaved accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We have to leave it at that for today. Mr. Nikolic, I thank you. I thank you also, Mr. Tansey, for bearing with us. We will resume tomorrow in the afternoon at 2.15. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 22nd day of April, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
